terms.definition: Identity and Access Management — a global, free AWS security service that controls authentication and authorization for all AWS resources.
terms.example: Like the security desk at an office that checks IDs and decides who can access which floors.

terms.definition: The original account owner identity created when an AWS account is first set up. Has unrestricted access to all services and resources.
terms.example: Like the master key to a building — powerful, but locked away and used only in emergencies.

terms.definition: An individual identity created within an AWS account for a specific person or application, with its own credentials and permissions.
terms.example: An employee ID card — belongs to one person, limits access based on their role.

terms.definition: A collection of IAM users that can share the same set of permissions. Policies attached to a group apply to all members.
terms.example: The 'Developers' team group — all developers automatically get the right tools when they join the group.

terms.definition: A JSON document that defines what actions are allowed or denied on which AWS resources. Attached to users, groups, or roles.
terms.example: Like a list of rules: 'This employee can enter rooms 1-3 but not the server room.'

terms.definition: A temporary, assumable identity used by AWS services, applications, or cross-account users. Has no permanent credentials — issues short-lived tokens.
terms.example: Like a visitor badge — anyone can use it for a limited time, and it expires automatically.

terms.definition: The process of verifying identity — proving who you are, typically via username and password or MFA.
terms.example: Scanning your employee ID card at the entrance — it proves you are who you say you are.

terms.definition: The process of determining what an authenticated identity is allowed to do — what resources it can access and what actions it can perform.
terms.example: After scanning your card, the system decides which floors you're allowed to enter.

terms.definition: Multi-Factor Authentication — requires two forms of verification: something you know (password) and something you have (a one-time code from a device).
terms.example: Like a bank card + PIN — knowing the PIN alone (password) isn't enough without the physical card (MFA device).

terms.definition: A security principle that states every identity should be granted only the minimum permissions necessary to perform its specific function.
terms.example: A cashier at a store can access the cash register but not the HR system or the manager's office.

terms.definition: A pair of credentials (Access Key ID + Secret Access Key) used for programmatic access to AWS via CLI, SDKs, or APIs.
terms.example: Like a username and password, but for code instead of browser logins.

terms.definition: A pre-built IAM policy created and maintained by AWS for common use cases. Can be attached to multiple users, groups, or roles.
terms.example: AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess — AWS writes it, you just attach it.

terms.definition: An IAM policy embedded directly into a single user, group, or role. Cannot be reused across multiple identities.
terms.example: A one-off exception policy written specifically for one contractor with unusual access needs.

terms.definition: An IAM policy statement with Effect: Deny. Always overrides any Allow statement, regardless of what other policies permit.
terms.example: A blacklist that beats a whitelist — if you're on the blocked list, no other permission can override it.

terms.definition: The maximum limit for a specific AWS resource or operation within an account or region. Formerly called service limits.
terms.example: A restaurant fire code limiting occupancy to 100 people — you can't seat more even if demand is there.

terms.definition: An AWS service quota that can be increased by submitting a quota increase request. Also called an adjustable quota.
terms.example: A hotel room cap that can be temporarily raised by calling ahead and getting approval.

terms.definition: An AWS service quota that is fixed and cannot be changed regardless of requests. An architectural constraint.
terms.example: A car with exactly 4 wheels — there's no option to add a 5th, it's how the design works.

terms.definition: An AWS tool that analyzes your account and provides automated recommendations across 5 categories: Cost, Performance, Security, Fault Tolerance, and Service Limits.
terms.example: Like a consultant who reviews your business and says 'You're wasting money here, and you have a security risk there.'

terms.definition: A dedicated AWS support engineer assigned to Enterprise support plan customers to provide proactive guidance and architectural advice.
terms.example: Having a personal trainer instead of just access to the gym — someone who knows your account and proactively helps you.

terms.definition: An account-specific AWS dashboard that shows events and notifications affecting your particular resources, as opposed to global AWS status.
terms.example: Your doctor sending you a personalized health report, vs reading the general public health news.

terms.definition: Five tiers of AWS customer support: Basic (free), Developer, Business, Enterprise On-Ramp, and Enterprise — each offering different response times and access levels.
terms.example: Like phone plans — you pay more for faster response times and more features.

terms.definition: An AWS tool that continuously monitors resource-based policies to identify any resources shared with external entities unexpectedly.
terms.example: A security audit tool that alerts you when someone accidentally left a door unlocked.
